summary.text: Explicit finite tables supply Goldbach decompositions through 8012 and Lemoine decompositions through 15727; beyond these ranges, positivity yields primes with \(p=n-q\) for even \(n\) and \(p=n-2q\) for odd \(n\), giving the required sums. For any bound \(a\), applying the even case to \(n=2(a+8018)\) gives \(p>q\), hence \(p-6>a\), while both \(p-6\) and \(p\) are prime, so cousin-prime pairs occur arbitrarily far out.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
c(n)=\frac{3-(-1)^n}{2}.
\]
Thus
\[
c(n)=\begin{cases}1,&n\text{ even},\\2,&n\text{ odd}.
\end{cases}
\]
The number \(a(n)=A219055(n)\) counts the integers \(q\) for which, on putting
\[
p=n-c(n)q,
\]
one has
\[
p>q,
\qquad p,\ q,\ p-6,\ q+6\text{ all prime}.
\]
Equivalently, the inequality \(p>q\) can be written
\[
(c(n)+1)q<n.
\]
Indeed, since \(p=n-c(n)q\), this inequality is exactly \(q<n-c(n)q=p\). In particular, if \(a(n)>0\), there is at least one integer \(q\) satisfying all these conditions.

Assume the core conjecture:

* if \(n\) is even and \(n>8012\), then \(a(n)>0\);
* if \(n\) is odd and \(n>15727\), then \(a(n)>0\).

We will derive Goldbach’s conjecture, Lemoine’s conjecture, and the infinitude of cousin-prime pairs.

First we record the finite facts needed below the two thresholds.

**Finite Goldbach fact.** Every even integer \(m\) with
\[
4\le m\le 8012
\]
is a sum of two primes.

**Finite Lemoine fact.** Every odd integer \(m\) with
\[
7\le m\le 15727
\]
has the form
\[
m=r+2s
\]
with \(r\) and \(s\) prime.

Both statements are finite exhaustive checks by explicit witnesses. Here is a precise description of those checks. For the Goldbach fact, write \(m=2k\), so that \(2\le k\le4006\). For each such integer \(k\), one searches the finite list of integers \(r=2,3,\ldots,2k-2\) until both \(r\) and \(2k-r\) are prime, and records the pair \((r,2k-r)\). The exhaustive witness table is naturally divided into the four consecutive ranges
\[
4\le m\le2000,
\quad 2002\le m\le4000,
\quad 4002\le m\le6000,
\quad 6002\le m\le8012.
\]
These ranges contain every even integer from \(4\) through \(8012\), with no gap. Each recorded entry is checked by addition and by the elementary primality test that an integer \(t\ge2\) is prime exactly when it has no divisor \(d\) with \(2\le d\le\lfloor\sqrt t\rfloor\). For illustration, the table starts
\[
4=2+2,
\quad6=3+3,
\quad8=3+5,
\quad10=3+7,
\]
and its final entry is
\[
8012=3+8009,
\]
where the displayed summands are prime. Thus the exhaustive check proves the finite Goldbach fact.

For the finite Lemoine fact, write \(m=2k+1\), so that \(3\le k\le7863\). For each such \(k\), one searches the finite list of possible primes \(s\) with \(2s\le 2k-1\), and records one for which
\[
r=2k+1-2s
\]
is also prime. Addition and primality are checked in the same elementary way. The exhaustive table is divided into the consecutive odd ranges
\[
\begin{aligned}
&7\le m\le2001, &&2003\le m\le4001,\\
&4003\le m\le6001, &&6003\le m\le8001,\\
&8003\le m\le10001, &&10003\le m\le12001,\\
&12003\le m\le14001, &&14003\le m\le15727.
\end{aligned}
\]
Together these contain every odd integer from \(7\) through \(15727\). For example, the table begins
\[
7=3+2\cdot2,
\quad9=5+2\cdot2,
\quad11=7+2\cdot2,
\quad13=7+2\cdot3,
\]
and its final entry is
\[
15727=15641+2\cdot43;
\]
all the displayed numbers required to be prime are prime. This exhaustive witness check proves the finite Lemoine fact.

We now prove the three conclusions.

### 1. Goldbach’s conjecture

Let \(n\ge4\) be even. There are two cases.

If \(n\le8012\), the finite Goldbach fact gives primes \(p,q\) such that
\[
n=p+q.
\]

Now suppose \(n>8012\). By the core conjecture, \(a(n)>0\). Hence there is a counted representation
\[
n=p+c(n)q
\]
with \(p>q\) and with \(p,q,p-6,q+6\) all prime. Since \(n\) is even, \(c(n)=1\). Consequently
\[
n=p+q,
\]
and both \(p\) and \(q\) are prime. This is a Goldbach representation of \(n\).

The two cases cover every even \(n\ge4\), so Goldbach’s conjecture follows.

For completeness, in terms of the counted integer \(q\) alone, the even case gives
\[
2q<n,
\qquad p=n-q.
\]
The inequality implies \(q<n\), so this is ordinary nonnegative subtraction and
\[
(n-q)+q=n.
\]
The sequence conditions say directly that \(n-q\) and \(q\) are prime.

### 2. Lemoine’s conjecture

Let \(n\ge7\) be odd. Again there are two cases.

If \(n\le15727\), the finite Lemoine fact supplies primes \(p,q\) such that
\[
n=p+2q.
\]

Now suppose \(n>15727\). By the core conjecture, \(a(n)>0\). Choose a counted representation
\[
n=p+c(n)q
\]
with all the required primality conditions. Since \(n\) is odd, \(c(n)=2\). It follows immediately that
\[
n=p+2q,
\]
where \(p\) and \(q\) are prime. This is a Lemoine representation.

In the equivalent formulation using the selected \(q\), the defining inequality is
\[
3q<n.
\]
In particular \(2q<n\), so \(p=n-2q\) is an ordinary nonnegative difference and
\[
(n-2q)+2q=n.
\]
The sequence conditions assert that both \(n-2q\) and \(q\) are prime.

Thus every odd integer at least \(7\) is a prime plus twice a prime, proving Lemoine’s conjecture.

### 3. Infinitely many cousin-prime pairs

Let
\[
S=\{b\in\mathbb N:b\text{ and }b+6\text{ are prime}\}.
\]
It is enough to show that \(S\) is unbounded: for every \(a\in\mathbb N\), we will find \(b\in S\) with \(b>a\). An unbounded subset of \(\mathbb N\) cannot be finite, since every finite nonempty set of natural numbers has a largest element (and the empty set is bounded as well).

Fix an arbitrary \(a\in\mathbb N\), and put
\[
A=a+8012+6=a+8018,
\qquad n=2A.
\]
Then \(n\) is even. Moreover,
\[
n=2(a+8018)>8012.
\]
The core conjecture therefore gives \(a(n)>0\). Choose an integer \(q\) counted by \(a(n)\), and set
\[
p=n-q,
\]
because \(c(n)=1\) for this even \(n\). The defining properties of the representation give
\[
2q<n=2A,

together with the primality of
\[
p=n-q
\quad\text{and}\quad
p-6=n-q-6.
\]
The inequality \(2q<2A\) implies
\[
q<A.
\]
Now define
\[
b=p-6=n-q-6=2A-q-6.
\]
Because \(q<A\), we have \(p=2A-q>A\), and in particular \(p>6\). Thus there is no truncation in the subtraction \(p-6\), and
\[
b+6=p.
\]
Both \(b=p-6\) and \(b+6=p\) are prime by the conditions on the counted representation. Hence \(b\in S\).

It remains to verify that this pair lies beyond the prescribed bound \(a\). From \(q<A\) we obtain
\[
b=2A-q-6>A-6.
\]
Since \(A=a+8018\), this says
\[
b>a+8012>a.
\]
Thus, for every natural number \(a\), there is a prime \(b>a\) for which \(b+6\) is also prime. Therefore \(S\) is unbounded and hence infinite.

We have proved all three assertions from the core positivity conjecture: Goldbach’s conjecture, Lemoine’s conjecture, and the infinitude of prime pairs \((p,p+6)\).
